summary: The Right rectangular pyramid calculator turns the base surface area, the lateral surface area and more into pyramid height (H). It is built for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Right rectangular pyramid calculator work?
sections.html:
The Right rectangular pyramid calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports pyramid height (H) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the base surface area (A_b), the lateral surface area (A_l), the volume (V) and the second lateral face area.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Right rectangular pyramid calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Pyramid height (H)=3 × volume (V) ÷ base surface area (A_b)
Base length (a)=base surface area (A_b) ÷ base width (b)
Base length (a)=2 × first lateral face area ÷ first slant height
Second slant height=2 × second lateral face area ÷ base width (b)
Total surface area (A)=base surface area (A_b) + 2 × first lateral face area + 2 × second lateral face area
Base length (a)=the square root of ((base diagonal − base width (b)) × (base diagonal + base width (b)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Right rectangular pyramid calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the base surface area, the lateral surface area and the volume — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Right rectangular pyramid calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns pyramid height (H), derived from the base surface area, the lateral surface area and the volume. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Right rectangular pyramid calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the base surface area, the lateral surface area, the volume and the second lateral face area, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter base length (a) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Base length (a) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Right rectangular pyramid calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
